title: Summary Ranges
statement:
`nums` holds distinct integers in increasing order. Break it into maximal runs of consecutive integers, where each value in a run is exactly one more than the value before it, and return one string per run, from left to right.

- A run that starts at `a` and ends at `b` with `a != b` is written `"a->b"`.
- A run of a single number `a` is written `"a"`.

Every number of `nums` belongs to exactly one run, and the runs contain no integer missing from `nums`. An empty `nums` gives an empty list.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
nums is sorted in increasing order
notes:
## Intuition

Because `nums` is sorted and has no repeats, a run of consecutive integers is always a contiguous stretch of the array: the next value either continues the run (it is one more) or starts a new one. So one left-to-right pass with two indices is enough: `start` marks where a run begins and `end` walks forward while the values keep stepping by exactly one. A brute-force alternative puts every value in a set and, from each value whose predecessor is missing, counts upward, but the sorted order makes that unnecessary.

## Approach

1. Create an empty list `ranges` and set `start = 0`.
2. While `start` is inside the array, set `end = start`.
3. Advance `end` while the next value equals `nums[end] + 1`.
4. If `start === end` the run is one number: push it on its own. Otherwise push `"nums[start]->nums[end]"`.
5. Jump `start` to `end + 1`, the first value not in this run, and repeat.
6. Return `ranges`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7]`.

- `start = 0`: `end` moves from index 0 to 2 (values 0, 1, 2); 4 is not 3, so it stops. Push `"0->2"`, then `start = 3`.
- `start = 3`: `end` moves to 4 (values 4, 5); 7 is not 6. Push `"4->5"`, then `start = 5`.
- `start = 5`: no next value, so `end = 5 = start`. Push `"7"`, then `start = 6` ends the loop.

The answer is `["0->2", "4->5", "7"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `end` only moves forward and `start` jumps past it, so each index is visited a constant number of times.
- Space: O(1) besides the output list.

## Pitfalls

- Test `end + 1 < nums.length` before reading `nums[end + 1]`, or the last run reads past the array.
- In fixed-width languages, `nums[end] + 1` overflows when `nums[end]` is `2^31 - 1`; compare with a wider type or check `nums[end + 1] - 1 == nums[end]` in 64 bits.
- A one-number run must be `"7"`, not `"7->7"`.
- An empty array returns an empty list; do not seed the loop with `nums[0]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ranges` | the strings produced so far |
| `start` | index where the current run begins |
| `end` | index of the last value in the current run |

narration.2: The answer list starts empty and fills one run at a time.
narration.3: start points at the first value of the run being built.
narration.5: Keep building runs until start has passed the last value.
narration.6: A run always contains at least its first value, so end begins at start.
narration.7: Extend the run while a next value exists and it is exactly one more than the current one.
narration.8: Step end onto that consecutive value.
narration.10: If end never moved, the run holds a single number.
narration.11: Write a single number on its own.
narration.13: Otherwise write the first and last values joined by an arrow.
narration.15: The next run begins right after this one ends.
narration.17: Every value now belongs to exactly one run; return the list.
